This book covers Bihar General Studies in full depth — geography, ancient and modern history, polity, economy, culture, personalities, government schemes, and tourism/heritage — built for the Bihar Public Service Commission (BPSC) and usable across all Bihar-based recruitment examinations that include a General Studies or Bihar GK component.

Eleven chapters combine full prose explanations, organized bullet points, and dedicated data tables — reflecting how genuinely dense this subject is: Bihar was the seat of India's first pan-subcontinental empire, the birthplace of Buddhism and Jainism's formative period, home to the ancient world's most celebrated universities, and the site of Gandhi's first Indian Satyagraha, alongside its modern political and economic story. Every chapter closes with a self-check quiz.

items: Read each chapter's opening narrative passages first for context, then use the bulleted sections and tables for structured revision and quick recall.
History carries the heaviest weightage in this subject — Chapters 2–4 (Ancient Magadha/Mauryas, Nalanda/Vikramshila, Medieval-Modern/Freedom Movement) deserve proportionally more study time.

This book was written in mid-2026 and reflects Bihar's very recent political transition (Samrat Choudhary succeeding Nitish Kumar as Chief Minister in April 2026) — treat all current officeholders and scheme figures as a snapshot and verify against a live source close to your exam date.
Use the data tables as your fastest revision tool in the final days before an exam — they consolidate the chapter's highest-yield facts in one scannable place.
Attempt each chapter's quiz without referring back to the notes, then review incorrect answers carefully.

blocks.content: Geography anchors nearly every other chapter in this book — the Ganga's division of the state, its flood-prone plains, and its administrative divisions recur constantly across BPSC and every other Bihar-based exam.

Bihar is a landlocked state in eastern India, bounded by Nepal to the north, West Bengal to the east, Uttar Pradesh to the west, and Jharkhand to the south — the last of these a relatively recent boundary, since Jharkhand was carved out of southern Bihar as a separate state only in November 2000. The state's defining geographical feature is the Ganga river, which flows west to east almost through the middle of the state, dividing it into two broad regions that differ in soil, drainage, and historical settlement pattern: North Bihar (the Ganga's northern plain, criss-crossed by Himalayan-fed rivers prone to severe seasonal flooding) and South Bihar (a comparatively drier plain grading into the Chota Nagpur plateau fringe near the Jharkhand border).

Almost the entire state lies within the fertile Indo-Gangetic plain, making Bihar's soil among the most agriculturally productive in India — but this same flat, low-lying terrain, combined with the state's location downstream of Himalayan rivers, also makes it one of the most flood-prone states in the country. North Bihar in particular experiences annual monsoon flooding from rivers like the Kosi, Gandak, and Bagmati, a recurring theme in both the state's economic planning and its disaster-management current affairs.

items: Bihar shares an international border with Nepal along its entire northern edge, making border-area administration and Indo-Nepal trade/security cooperation a recurring subject in the state's polity and current-affairs coverage.

The state is divided by the Ganga into North Bihar and South Bihar; North Bihar is generally flatter and more flood-prone, while South Bihar has slightly more elevated and undulating terrain, especially near the Jharkhand plateau fringe.

A small hilly tract exists in the southern part of the state (parts of Jamui, Nawada, Gaya, and neighbouring districts), representing the northern extension of the Chota Nagpur plateau system, in contrast to the otherwise overwhelmingly flat alluvial character of the state.

Bihar's total geographical area is comparatively modest among Indian states, but it is one of the most densely populated, with population density figures consistently among the highest of any Indian state — a fact with direct bearing on land-use, agriculture, and urbanization questions.

The Ganga is Bihar's principal river, entering from Uttar Pradesh near Buxar and flowing eastward through the state before continuing into West Bengal; nearly all of Bihar's other major rivers are tributaries that eventually join the Ganga.

North Bihar's rivers — including the Gandak, Kosi, Bagmati, Kamla Balan, and Mahananda — originate in the Himalayas (mostly in Nepal) and are notorious for their shifting courses and severe monsoon flooding; the Kosi in particular is often called the 'Sorrow of Bihar' for its history of dramatic course changes and destructive floods.

South Bihar's rivers — including the Son, Punpun, and Falgu — are comparatively less flood-prone but face significant dry-season water scarcity, since they are rain-fed rather than glacier/snow-fed like the northern rivers.
The Son river, one of the Ganga's major southern tributaries, is notable for the Indrapuri Barrage and its role in irrigating substantial parts of South Bihar.

Bihar has a humid subtropical climate with hot summers, a monsoon season (roughly June to September) that brings the bulk of annual rainfall, and a relatively mild winter — broadly similar to the climate pattern across much of the Indo-Gangetic plain.

The state's alluvial soil, deposited over centuries by the Ganga and its tributaries, is highly fertile and supports Bihar's position as a major agricultural producer, particularly for rice, wheat, maize, and a range of fruits and vegetables.

Flooding and drought can occur in the same state within the same broad region in different years (or even different parts of the state in the same year), given the contrast between the flood-prone north and the comparatively drought-vulnerable south — a distinguishing feature of Bihar's geography frequently tested in comparative questions.

Exam Tip

• The North Bihar/South Bihar divide by the Ganga, and the flood-prone North vs comparatively drought-vulnerable South distinction, is the single most consistently tested geographic concept for Bihar exams — know it well beyond simple memorization.

• The Kosi river's nickname ('Sorrow of Bihar') and its history of course changes is a guaranteed recurring exact-fact question.

• Divisional headquarters and their constituent districts (Table 1.1) are frequently tested via direct matching questions — a quick memorization pass on this table pays off disproportionately.

blocks.content: Q1. Which river divides Bihar into North Bihar and South Bihar?
Q2. Which Bihar river is popularly known as the 'Sorrow of Bihar' due to its shifting course and destructive floods?
Q3. Jharkhand was carved out of southern Bihar as a separate state in which year?
Q4. The Indrapuri Barrage, supporting irrigation in South Bihar, is located on which river?
Q5. Compared to North Bihar, South Bihar's rivers are generally:
B. Less flood-prone but more prone to dry-season water scarcity
C. Entirely dry throughout the year
D. Larger in volume than North Bihar's rivers
Answer: Less flood-prone but more prone to dry-season water scarcity
